title: What’s Quebec identity anyway? These Quebecers had a lot to say | CBC News
text:
There are two words that always seem to come up in political discourse in this province: Quebec identity or, in French, l’identité Québécoise.

But what does it mean? Who defines it? Ahead of the Oct. 5 provincial election, I asked a cross section of Quebecers — and they offered a wealth of perspectives.

What follows is a series of those candid and nuanced conversations. I chatted with two women who left India and Pakistan in the 1970s for Quebec under René Lévesque. I met young sovereignists with Indigenous and Maghrebi roots, respectively.

I also caught up with one woman who identifies as a Montrealer — not a Quebecer — and two others who told me how they juggle their Quebec pride while fervently defending their English-language institutions.

Here's what they had to say.

Protecting language shapes her identity as a trilingual Tamil Quebecer

A born-and-raised Montrealer, 25-year-old Krishnavi Sivanesan spends her weekends teaching Tamil to a group of younger people, who often speak to each other in French while in class.

Sivanesan says she understands Quebec's fight to protect the French language, given that her family fled war-torn Sri Lanka because they struggled there to live their lives as Tamils.

But she feels the common political discourse about non-Francophones and immigrants don't take her community's contributions into account.

What does Quebec identity mean to these women with South Asian roots?

Quebec has been home to Dolores Chew and Shaheen Ashraf for more than 50 years. And they still enjoy South Asian comforts like a cup of chai.

Over tea and snacks, they fondly recall a Quebec under René Lévesque. One of them voted ‘Yes’ in the 1980 referendum. But their sense of belonging changed after that.

2 sovereignists — with Moroccan and Indigenous roots — explain why Quebec should be a country

Nabil Ben Ali Ouriaghli and Benjamin Gingras are both members of Oui Quebec, a citizen-led movement promoting sovereignty. They say their vision of an independent Quebec is one that focuses on inclusion and what brings people together.

But they recognize there’s work to do in getting that message out.

Why this Montrealer’s identity is rooted in the city – and not in Quebec and Canada

Western Canada didn’t quite feel like home, but Montreal sure did.

When Shereen Joseph moved to the Plateau-Mont-Royal borough, she found the identity that truly resonated with her: Montrealer. She explains how her Malaysian roots helped her embrace the city and the French language — and why the language tensions in this province seem so foreign.

What Quebec identity means to these 2 bilingual English school board commissioners

For Susan Perera and Allison Saunders, English-language schools are not just about education, they’re also about community and promoting a bilingual Quebec.

Both English school board commissioners proudly claim their Quebec identity. But at times, Saunders feels she "does not tick all the boxes" when it comes to how some people define what it means to be a Quebecer.

Sudha Krishnan is a host with CBC Montreal.  She is an award-winning journalist who has reported from Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario. Born in Montreal, Sudha is a proud alumna of the Concordia University journalism department.
